content.text:
17 passing, types clean. Now the refactor analysis.

**Naming evaluation (first priority)**

- `withPolicyModifiers(policyBase, customer)` — the name says "with policy modifiers", but the body applies exactly one of the two policy modifiers by name (`withFirstInsuranceSurcharge`) and inlines the other (loyalty). The name is accurate but the body is asymmetric.
- `withFirstInsuranceSurcharge` — this is a *policy* modifier, but it sits up next to `basePremium` far from `withPolicyModifiers`, named as a wrapper (`with…`) while loyalty is a summand. Two policy modifiers, two different shapes.
- Everything else (`groupBasePremium`, `itemSurcharges`, `isLongStanding`, `percentOf`, `roundPremium`) reads well and matches what the tests demand.

So the naming defect is **inconsistent shape between two members of the same concept**, not a wrong word.

**Rule 2 (reveals intent) — the finding**

The file's own comment states the domain law: *"Both are ADDITIVE against the base rather than compounding, so they are summed side by side and never nested inside one another."* But `withFirstInsuranceSurcharge` **is** nested inside — `base + percentOf(base, …)` is a wrapper, contradicting the stated law in shape even though it agrees in arithmetic. A reader must verify the equivalence by hand to see the two modifiers are peers.

Making first-insurance a summand like loyalty makes the law visible in the code:

content.text:
All 17 green, types clean.

**On the unification question you flagged** — I judged a policy-modifier table **not** warranted, and deliberately did not build one. Your warning was correct and it is worth recording *why*, because the reason is stronger than "it's premature":

The two policy modifiers I made symmetric are symmetric *in arithmetic shape* (percent of policy base, summed). They are not symmetric in **what they are predicated on**. First-insurance is unconditional; loyalty depends on the customer; follow-up will depend on the step index. A `(customer) => boolean` table would fit exactly one of the three. A table generalized far enough to hold all three (`(customer, stepIndex) => boolean`) would be a table whose every row ignores most of its own parameters — more elements (Rule 4) and less intent (Rule 2) than three named summands. The refactoring I did captures the real shared structure (additive percent-of-base) without inventing a false shared predicate.

**APP mass**

`withPolicyModifiers` + `withFirstInsuranceSurcharge` before: constants 0, bindings 6, invocations 4 (=8), conditionals 1 (=4) → **18**.
`policyModifiers` after: constants 1, bindings 6, invocations 3 (=6), conditionals 1 (=4) → **17**. `policyPremium` gained one binding (+1) by naming `policyBase` instead of calling `itemsBasePremium` inline — but it also dropped an invocation (−2), so net **−1** there too.

Mass barely moved, and that is the honest result: this refactoring was bought under Rule 2, not APP. The gain is that the file no longer contradicts itself. The comment asserted modifiers are "summed side by side and never nested inside one another" while `withFirstInsuranceSurcharge` nested one inside the base. A reader had to expand `base + percentOf(base, 10)` by hand to confirm the two modifiers were really peers.

**One thing to watch when follow-up lands.** `policyModifiers` currently takes `(policyBase, customer)`. Follow-up needs the step index, which `quote` has access to only if `runScenario` passes it — `scenario.steps.map((step) => ...)` currently discards the index. So the next Green phase will need to thread an index through `runScenario -> quote -> policyPremium -> policyModifiers`, the same way this one threaded `Customer`. That is a signature change on four functions, not a new branch in one. If a third thread-through appears after that, the signal is to bundle `{ customer, stepIndex }` into a named `QuoteContext` type — but two is not yet enough to justify it.
